items.title: The surprising science of awe — and what it reveals about consciousness
items.summary: Years ago on the way to New Zealand for my doctoral studies, I stopped in Los Angeles to visit a friend. He organized a trip to Joshua Tree, where we hiked and camped. Come nightfall, I gazed at the stars and clouds — or so I thought. My friend pointed out that the cloudcover was, in fact, the Milky Way. I didn’t realize our galaxy was ever visible to the naked eye, and I was deeply moved. The vast stillness of the desert, the free-roaming coyotes and the thick blanket of stars reminded me that we humans are only a tiny part of it all, yet also unbreakably connected to this stretching, expansive universe. More than a decade later, the awe of that experience remains important and vivid in my life. Panoramic view of the Milky Way arch over Joshua trees in the Mojave Desert. Viktor Skalican / Alamy Now, as a psychological scientist, I study awe for a living. Last summer, my colleagues and I asked 200 people in the UK to document their encounters with awe over six weeks. Because such experiences are often linked to a sense of purpose and flourishing, we wanted to know what mattered more: their frequency or intensity. What we found surprised us. As we explain in this John Templeton Foundation-supported paper , those who experienced moments of awe that induced strong feelings of amazement and wonder reported a greater sense of meaning and wellbeing by the study’s end. It wasn’t how often people felt awe that mattered, but whether they had an experience which strongly evoked it. What, exactly, happens to us when we experience awe, and what makes the feeling so significant, in such a lasting way? We researchers know that it has something to do with feeling simultaneously small and connected to something larger. During awe, analytical thinking recedes; we simply experience , transcending the cerebral way in which we ordinarily engage with the world. After years investigating this phenomenon, I’ve come to believe that awe offers a window into an overlooked aspect of human consciousness — one of science’s most elusive mysteries. If we can isolate and study the state of awe and similar self-transcendent experiences, we might deepen our understanding of our species, and of how we experience the world. The problem with the thinking mind When we think of consciousness, we imagine a conscious voice that says, “This is now” — an idea that goes back at least as far as the 17 th -century French philosopher René Descartes, who famously stated, “I think, therefore I am.” But what if this thinking (literally) has led us astray? My inquiry into consciousness started in 2015, when I began researching analytical versus intuitive thinking. Having trained as a cognitive neuroscientist during my PhD at the University of Auckland in New Zealand, I’d always prioritized the rational mind, dismissing intuition as a lesser agency — one reserved for guessing games or New Age spirituality. It’s a predictable bias: Since Descartes, the Enlightenment and the Scientific Revolution, much of Western culture has privileged logic over the supposedly mercurial feelings of the body. It wasn’t until I began working with Dr. Miguel Farias on the psychology of religion and spirituality that I questioned my assumptions about intuition. Our research challenged the idea that religious belief is necessarily rooted in intuitive rather than analytical thinking, and made me reconsider whether the preference for rational thought might be limiting how we understand the human mind. Even for an academic like me, who saw the body mostly as a way to transport my brain from place to place, experiences of awe like the one I had at Joshua Tree seemed too consequential to ignore. Research suggests that intuition plays an important role in how we perceive the world and make decisions, even when we’re not consciously aware of the processes guiding us. In a foundational study , neuroscientists Antoine Bechara, Antonio Damasio and their colleagues asked participants to choose cards from four decks — two advantageous and two disadvantageous. They found that subjects began showing subtle physiological signs of stress when approaching the unfavorable decks, even before they could consciously identify them as risky. The researchers interpreted these findings as evidence that the body can influence decisions before we can consciously explain them. Psychologist Jonathan Haidt has made a similar argument about moral judgment, likening the rational mind to a press secretary: Rather than making decisions, the brain may simply explain and justify conclusions we’ve already reached intuitively. In a way it makes sense: Working memory, which supports analytical thinking, has a limited capacity. Yet there is a whole world around us that we need to take in, which the body does holistically through its various senses. For me, these findings raised a larger question: How much of our experience of the world unfolds beyond the reach of reflective thought? And if we fail to fully study this intuitive, non-reflective dimension of our minds, how complete can our understanding of consciousness really be? The self that thinking cannot capture This question brought me back to an idea proposed more than a century ago by William James, widely regarded as the father of modern psychology. In his 1892 text, Psychology: Briefer Course , James distinguished between two aspects of the self, which he called the “Me” and the “I”: “Whatever I may be thinking of, I am always at the same time more or less aware of myself, of my personal existence. At the same time it is I who am aware; so that the total self of me, being as it were duplex, partly known and partly knower, partly object and partly subject, must have two aspects discriminated in it, of which for shortness we may call one the Me and the other the I.” In line with philosophical discussions , I developed modern definitions for the two aspects of James’s “total self.” His “Me” is what I call the reflective self-state: conscious awareness, where we think about ourselves, reflect on what we are doing or have done, interpret how we are perceived, and so on. It’s the type of thinking that can be described in language, and thus be made explicit. James’s “I” is what I have come to think of as the experiential self-state: the part of us that simply is — in the here and now, as a sensing entity. The experiential self-state is difficult to describe, because the moment we try to put it into words we shift toward the reflective self-state, making ourselves the object of our attention once again. But this doesn’t mean the experiential self is simply an absence of thought or intention. Rather, it’s a form of awareness in which bodily sensations, emotions and sensory information come together to guide our perceptions and responses, without deliberate thought. Deep meditation offers a useful example of the experiential self-state, as does awe. What science might be missing about awe This distinction between reflective and experiential awareness could help resolve a longstanding puzzle in the study of awe itself. To measure the awe we feel during concerts, psychedelic trips, collective rituals, mystical encounters and the like, researchers use the Awe Experience Scale (AWE-S) , a survey tool developed by Johns Hopkins University psychologist David Yaden and his colleagues. I’ve used this scale extensively in my own research , and encountered a recurring puzzle. Participants sometimes describe feeling small or insignificant during awe, as I did at Joshua Tree, only for that sensation to give way to an overwhelming sense of connection. I wonder whether retrospective surveys capture this lasting connectedness more readily than the fleeting feeling of self-diminishment. items.title: The Loneliness of Buying Too Many Things
items.summary: Maybe you remember them: the credit-card offers—so congratulatory, so seductive—that pour into graduating college seniors’ mailboxes. To the unwary, they seem to promise free money. In practice, they can often lead to debt. This is what happens to Becky Bloomwood, the protagonist of the chick-lit classic Confessions of a Shopaholic , by the British writer Sophie Kinsella. The novel opens with a bank offering Becky an extended overdraft of £2,000 for her first two years in the workforce. Mere pages later, the two years are up, and Becky, now a financial journalist with a serious shopping habit, owes the bank thousands of pounds. Confessions of a Shopaholic came out in the United States 25 years ago, and certain aspects of the book haven’t aged at all: Becky’s chatty warmth is as enjoyable as ever, and the debt she racks up will likely be relatable to as many readers now as in the early aughts. But the details and texture of her shopping—physical credit cards swiped, department stores wandered through—are so unlike the reality of today’s consumerism, with its smartphones and scrolling, that the novel is almost a time capsule. Becky’s eagerness, her longing, and her bubbly charisma made Confessions of a Shopaholic a hit when it was published—surprising, perhaps, for a comic novel about a woman with a shopping addiction. Although it received hardly any critical attention, it was, along with Helen Fielding’s Bridget Jones’s Diary and Lauren Weisberger’s The Devil Wears Prada , core to one of the most popular genres of its time. Yet, unlike some of its peers, Confessions of a Shopaholic is a fundamentally solitary, even lonely, book. Becky’s focus on shopping crowds out other characters. Perhaps this is why the novel’s film adaptation hasn’t endured; contrast it with those of Bridget Jones’s Diary and The Devil Wears Prada , which have surpassed the books themselves. Fielding’s and Weisberger’s novels revolve around friendship, romance, or careers that involve collaborating with others—all relationships that are easy to dramatize on-screen. But the central relationship in Confessions of a Shopaholic is Becky’s connection to, and yearning for, material things. She’s at her most emotional when shopping, which, with very few exceptions, she does alone. As a result, the book’s most captivating sections are internal monologues directed at objects that can’t want Becky back. The adaptation, starring Isla Fisher, does its best to create new versions of these moments—in one scene, a mannequin talks to Becky—but it doesn’t capture the book’s real drama, which is inside its heroine’s head. If Confessions of a Shopaholic had been written in 2026, Becky would be more solitary still—so alone that the novel might not work at all. Kinsella, who died late last year, was gifted at buoying readers along through the sheer power of voice, but even she might not have been able to make a charming, compelling read out of a woman scrolling through pages and pages of buyable things on her phone. In fact, reading the novel today is at once a reminder of how much shopping has changed and a grim preview of what was to come: As consumers, at least, we’re all as alone as Becky Bloomwood now. Confessions of a Shopaholic does have characters other than its heroine. Kinsella introduces readers to Becky’s parents; her supremely posh roommate, Suze; a fellow financial journalist, Elly, who shares Becky’s interest in fashion; the bank and credit-card-account managers who pursue her; and, naturally, her enemy turned love interest, a communications mogul and Eligible Bachelor named Luke Brandon. Yet these characters don’t speak all that much, and, though it’s clear to the reader that she needs some intervention, the only ones who challenge her are calling to collect debt. That the people around Becky never help her is part of the novel’s plot, not a failure of its writing. Kinsella demonstrates that Becky learned her acquisitiveness from her mother, and also gives enough (very funny) detail about Suze’s upper-class background that readers will understand why she’s too clueless to help her friend rein in her wild spending. In fact, Suze’s wealth lets her enable Becky: She’s rich enough to give her roommate breaks from the rent. The only person who can meaningfully confront Becky about her shopping habit is Becky herself, but for all her anxiety about overextending herself financially, that’s not something she intends to do. “If everyone could just wear new clothes every day,” Becky muses, “I reckon depression wouldn’t exist anymore”—and readers know she believes this is true. [ Read: A better way of buying—and wanting—things ] In 2026, a shopaholic like Becky could blow their earnings on the internet. Becky spends her money—and her time—out in the world. She tells the reader, “There’s a thrill about walking into a shop—any shop—which you can’t beat.” The novel’s tensest interactions, the ones most loaded with desire and expectation, take place between Becky and store employees who don’t know her name. It’s these women (and they’re always women) who see her most vulnerable self. In an early scene, Becky begs an employee at a luxury store to hold a marked-down scarf behind the register for her; she’s left her credit card at work and will have to go get it. Over the course of this conversation, her face “flames red”; she speaks “quickly,” “desperately,” and “beseechingly.” When the shopgirl eventually agrees to reserve the scarf until that evening, Becky is overcome with “a combination of relief and adrenaline.” Kinsella’s prose here makes exceedingly clear that Becky doesn’t just have a cute shopping problem. It’s an addiction that—even if Becky’s friends and family don’t clock it—is on public display. Kinsella doesn’t blame her heroine for her predicament; Confessions of a Shopaholic , for all its effervescence, is a straightforward critique of consumer culture. Becky is a decidedly unreflective character: She does not have—or seem inclined to develop—the self-awareness to examine the world of deals and sales and reward points that she inhabits. But the novel knows from the start that these bargains are traps, such as the supposedly no-strings-attached overdraft offer that gets Becky in trouble. Throughout the book, various moments of visceral longing—Becky says of a pair of £90 zebra-print jeans: “If you were in Gucci, you’d be paying at least £500. Oh God, I want them, I want them”—make obvious that Becky, living amid all the shops of London, is effectively a gambler in a city of slot machines. She’s surrounded by temptation, and there’s always some way not to say no. [ Read: ] A close-up look at the waste of modern life But this is chick lit, not Uncut Gems . Confessions of a Shopaholic still ends happily, with Becky landing a rich boyfriend and a lucrative job. With her new salary, she’ll be able to pay off her overdraft and keep shopping—and Kinsella dangles the promise that soon, Becky will have a wealthy husband to foot her bills. In short, Becky’s problems are solved, yet she remains on the isolated treadmill of her compulsions: want new things, buy new things, repeat. A contemporary Becky would arguably have an even easier time continuing to shop, and a harder time resisting. She’d have a smartphone in her pocket, overflowing with tempting sale offers and the promise of buy-now-pay-later services that encourage people—especially women, as my colleague Annie Joy Williams has reported —to spend even further beyond their means than credit cards already do. Most likely, it would also be full of posts and messages from influencers who recommend products to their followers in casual, effusive tones—not unlike the voice that Kinsella gives Becky. In a sense, the Shopaholic movie got something right with that talking mannequin: Like the TikTokers and Substackers making money from their followers’ clicks and purchases, the mannequin allows Becky to feel like she’s shopping with a friend when,

items.title: Mom Is in Her Shapeshifting Era
items.summary: The Original Mother The original mother brought out the toenail clippers and sat cross-legged in front of the La-Z-Boy, steadying her husband’s narrow foot with her left hand, his calloused heel wedged in her palm. His eyes were pointed at the TV. Jeopardy . “Who was it?” he asked. There had been a knock at the door a short while ago. “A man.” “Huh.” “Selling fish from a pole,” the original mother said. Her husband dug at his jaw. “Who is Vasco . . .” he said. “Vasco da Gama!” “Is that his name?” Her husband’s face fell. “Huh?” “The man,” the original mother said, suddenly finding herself curious for anything that might shed light on the stranger that had come to their door. “Does he sell fish here often? Vasco?” “Oh, right,” her husband said, concentrating on the next clue. “Sure.” He wriggled his toes. His ankle let out a frivolous little crack. They lapsed into silence. The original mother pursed her lips and tried to clip his gray toenails, but the hot ache in her old, arthritic fingers was too much to bear. “Ah . . . oh! What is the Law of Reflection?” her husband said. The original mother let her eyes go soft. Her husband’s toes grew indistinct. As she reckoned with the crude geometry of this latest defeat, another woman, her mirror image, brought out a second pair of toenail clippers, sat cross-legged before the La-Z-Boy, and steadied the husband’s other foot with her right hand. The original mother’s husband jerked the legrest down and grasped both women by their wrists, shaking the toenail clippers from their hands. The mothers appraised each other and said, “Who are you?” Then they looked at their husband, gawking at them like a carp. He tightened his grip and held on well past the evening news. The second woman coughed harshly and then, quite astonishingly, crumpled in on herself, until a fox emerged from the folds of a uniform of a mother. “Get out of here,” her husband growled. The fox regarded the original mother before bolting out the door through the pet flap, unused since the beagle’s death, but the original mother hadn’t seen a thing. She’d made herself absent, her eyes shut tight to brace against the pain of her husband’s grip, but also to better heed her heart. Remarkable, the way it beat! The original mother’s older brother came to visit, the first time in nearly forty years, spurred by their younger sister’s coming-out message in their otherwise uneventful group chat on KakaoTalk. When he arrived, his shirttail got caught in the taxi’s door, the tiny wheels of his mean aluminum suitcase burst asunder over a crack, and he immediately stubbed his toe on the doorjamb. “Sister,” he said, between dramatic breaths and staring incredulously at the pet flap, “what is this? This American existence?” The original mother knew why he had really come: to lay bare his love and resentment to the woman for whom he had long nursed a quiet crush, foolishly believing her to be nothing more than their younger sister’s best friend. It didn’t matter that he was old, that they were all old, the geometry of their ways long set fast. He had come to make a point. He would have the original mother drive him a short distance to the sister’s apartment, where he’d condemn her for the wickedness of homosexuality, disown her in the same breath, and then turn his frustrations on the original mother, enumerating all the ways American life had tarnished her character. As the original mother cooked him a lavish meal, she flung open the windows to air the house so her husband wouldn’t carp about the smell of their “exotic” food encroaching on his enjoyment of Jeopardy . “My hands are dry, sister.” She gave her brother almond-scented hand lotion, envying the straightness of his fingers. “I’m thirsty,” he whined. She handed him a glass of cold water. “America has made you fatter than you should be.” The bean curd stew boiled furiously. The stuffed perilla leaves steamed into her face. Her brother proceeded to explain how she was to blame for, well, everything. He had an enlarged prostate and had developed an irrational fear of death, and even that was her fault. “I’m hungry. I’m hungry.” Just as she set down the bowl of rice, another hand, not her own, placed a bowl of rice beside it. It belonged to a woman who looked exactly like her. They stood at the table and appraised each other and said, “Who are you?” Then they looked at their brother, glaring incandescently at them like a lacquered scorpion. “Ahn-nyah! Now, sister, what is this?” Her brother’s eyes narrowed as he ripped into her for such brazen chicanery. Only in America, he fumed, would a brother be served a dinner conjured by some kind of black magic, almost certainly purchased on Amazon. He shouted so loudly that the original mother’s husband had to crank up the TV. Her brother shouted well past the evening news. The second mother plugged her ears with her fingers, then puffed out her cheeks and emitted an uncanny whine. The sound was enough to stop the original mother’s brother mid-rant. As the air escaped the woman’s body, she crumpled in on herself, quite miraculously, until a fox emerged from the folds of a uniform of a mother. “Get out of here,” her brother growled. The original mother hadn’t seen a thing. She’d made herself absent, her eyes shut tight to brace against her brother’s words, but also to better heed her heart. Remarkable, the way it beat! The original mother once had a mother, and her mother a mother as well, the uniform of the original mother passing from one generation to the next. Earlier, her son had called, but she wasn’t in the right mindset to answer, crushed, as she was, by the geometry of her exhaustion. She should have answered, or at least called back. Now, an intrusive guilt keeps her awake long after the late-night news. The original mother blinks into the dark, thinking. If her son had answered the door, he would have bought a fish from—what was his name again? She opens her mouth very slightly and focuses on the puckered shadow cast by the curtain, situating herself in the moment the name was spoken. Finally, it comes to her, bright as happiness: Vasco. Her son, keen to avoid confrontation in any form and unwilling to risk seeming an inconvenience to anyone but his mother, would have taken one look at Vasco, spun a private story about his troubles, and bought a fish, because who went around selling fish like that? He would have carried it inside and left it in its taut plastic bag on the kitchen counter beside the instant coffee and her husband’s glazed donuts, where she would have had to contend with the fish’s pouting mouth and its eyes, gaping up at her in troubled amazement. Her son’s birth had been a very difficult one. The original mother eases out from under the sheets, pads past the extraordinary sounds of her husband’s snoring, past her brother’s faltering puffs and snorts, and pauses before the cheval mirror, an heirloom from her husband’s mother, and the only thing her brother allowed any measure of approval as he wended unbidden through every room, drumming his index finger against his lips. Even in the dark, she sees the woman standing on the other side who looks exactly like her. She is wholly present now, heeds her heart—remarkable, the way it beats! She slips into the utility room and opens the drawer that only a mother would ever think to open, a drawer that only a mother would even know exists. From beneath a bright orange box of dryer sheets, she pulls out a uniform of a fox. She contorts into it, her joints and muscles screaming, thinking all the while, “When will it be done?” It is done. She will return before sunrise, before the morning news, to resume her duties as the original mother, of course. But until then, the night is hers. She darts through the pet flap—but not before appraising the woman in the mirror—and vanishes tenderly into the dark. The post Mom Is in Her Shapeshifting Era appeared first on Electric Literature .

items.title: Two Trans Novelists Have Broken the National Book Awards’ Glass Ceiling
items.summary: Tonight the winners of the 77th National Book Awards will be announced. Though this will be published before we know which authors ultimately receive the grand honor, I already know that the finalists this year uniquely—and with exquisite, hard-earned artistic merit—speak to the ever-evolving state of American literature. Two of the finalists for the National Book Award in Fiction are trans—only the second and third openly trans authors ever to be nominated in this category. At no fault of trans writers, and all fault of the societal powers that be: This simply was not possible even a decade ago. If we’re not careful, it might not be possible once again, even before the next presidential term. It’s for this reason, additional to the fact of their literary genius, that I consider myself greatly privileged to spotlight National Book Award finalists Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera. From untangling the increasingly hostile and anti-trans US political landscape in Thomas’s Mad Eden , to exploring Colombia’s lively queer underground scene in Lopera’s Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You , both of these authors’ novels prove to be unprecedented in craft, and unchallengeably excellent. Over Zoom, email, and voice notes, Thomas, Lopera, and I discussed the complexity of labels in trans and neurodivergent communities, the nuances of capturing queer joy, and the difficult onus of representation for minority authors. Jalen Giovanni Jones: So first, I’d like to congratulate you both on the many accolades that these beautiful novels brought you, particularly you both being finalists for the National Book Award! That is such a huge accomplishment. We’ll dive into craft and form shortly, but tell me—how has it felt, receiving these honors? How have you celebrated yourself? Morgan Thomas: For me, I felt really grateful to the selection committee for choosing two books that have trans and gender expansive themes. If they had chosen just one, it would be easy for it to feel like there was one specific trans story that was being legitimized. Choosing two feels like a really beautiful thing for them to have done at this moment. So I feel really grateful. Right when I heard the finalist list and understood that there were two trans books on it, mixed in with that happiness and gratitude was a sense of . . . frustration is too strong, but something that recognized the fact that there are so many incredible trans writers who have been super impactful for me, and who my work is deeply indebted to, who I wish had gotten this accolade over the many years that have passed already. Writers who immediately come to mind include Sabrina Imbler, Zeyn Joukhadar, Jordy Rosenberg, Torrey Peters, Katherine Packert Burke. There are so many more. I want to see all of them receive the accolades, the attention, and the incredible things that they deserve. To be an immigrant in this country, and to write this book that is very trans, very Colombian, that has so much Spanish in it, and to have it received this way—it feels incredible. Julián Delgado Lopera: It’s been so surreal for me, and so amazing. My body has been so excited that I got sick both times. The first time, when I was longlisted, I had a headache for 10 days. And then I had a stomach bug when I was shortlisted. I came [to the US] when I was 15 years old and barely knew English, so I had to explain to my mom what the National Book Awards [are]. To be an immigrant in this country, and to write this book that is very trans, very Colombian, that has so much Spanish in it, and to have it received this way—it feels incredible. JGJ: Both of your novels explore how queer joy can persevere under oppressive conditions. In Mad Eden , they survive through safe havens like Ro and Liam’s home, and shared online spaces. In Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You , it lives through the queer underground scene. Were these sanctuaries ones that you had experienced in your personal life? When did it occur to you that you wanted to capture such sanctuaries of queer joy in your novel? MT: 100 percent. Small, queer community spaces—both online and in-person—have definitely been sites of joy for me, and also sites of rest and support through hard times. I knew I wanted to include those themes when I started writing the novel in early 2023. As someone working in public health focused on Two Spirit and LGBTQ+ health equity work at the time, I found myself talking a lot about joy. I was doing interviews for blog articles, we would be talking about state laws that were making it harder to access gender affirming care, and the slew of anti-trans legislation that was happening at the state level, and then at the end I would find myself being like, “What’s one thing that’s made you feel okay this week?” I think it came from a place of wanting to highlight resilience and also to remind ourselves and each other that there are small things we can do to stay grounded. But at some point I was like, “Why have I become like a salesperson for joy? Why am I just constantly insisting that people feel joyful and talk to me about joy?” I thought about the way that sometimes joy and happiness are expected, or even demanded, of trans people as a way of validating their gender identity, and I heard a similar insistence in myself. So I really just wanted to both highlight the incredible amount of joy that does exist in queer and trans communities, in spite of whatever legislative stuff is going on, and then at the same time ask myself what [it’s] like when those emotions [are] also complicated and how they can be complicated among trans folks and specifically within that sort of public health space. Sometimes joy and happiness are expected, or even demanded, of trans people as a way of validating their gender identity, and I heard a similar insistence in myself. JDL: Yes and no. For Pretend You’re Dead and I Carry You , some of it comes from my life, and some just stories that I’ve heard from people. Tia Mama, the big travesti matriarch that comes into the story, is based on my own trans mother, who passed away two years ago. Her name was Adela Vazquez. She became that haven for me when I didn’t talk to my family after I ran away to San Francisco when I was 20. Through her, I met a larger queer family, a bunch of elders that came into my life. That familial structure that Ignacio finds in the Electrica Family was [based on] something I knew very well from San Francisco, but also from stuff other people [told] me. I also went to Columbia in 2019 and did research on the trans history there, through mostly oral storytelling and people telling me stuff, and then also watching videos and photographs. In the novel I was building on the familiar structures that I had read and heard about. A lot of my experience with queer families comes from the life I built in a very underground, queer San Francisco, and for the novel I paired it with the research that I did on Columbia. JGJ: Both Mad Eden and Pretend You’re Dead are incredibly complex, form-wise. With Mad Eden , you were weaving together traditional narrative with chapters of the online Mad Eden (the fantasy serial “book” within the book), social media posts, emails. With Pretend You’re Dead , we’re presented with two different timelines relayed to us across multiple different narrators. Was your novel always going to be so formally ambitious in this way? MT: It wasn’t. The form came really late in the writing process, but I had backed myself into the form that it ended up having. My writing process isn’t linear, so essentially I had written a scene here, a scene there. I knew I wanted these two characters to have this conversation. items.title: How Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day
items.summary: As of November 18, 2026, if you send a signal out at the speed of light in the direction of Voyager 1 — humanity’s most distant spacecraft — it will now take more than a full day for that signal to arrive . At that impressive distance, more than three times the distance to Pluto, over 16 billion miles, and over 25.9 billion kilometers away, the Sun appears 30,000 times fainter than it does from Earth. (That’s still brighter than the full Moon, but only by a factor of 14, or under three astronomical magnitudes.) It’s moving away from the Sun at a current speed of 60,770 km/hr (37,760 mph), and has reached that one light-day milestone after a cumulative journey of 49 years and 72 days. In all the years since 1977, we’ve never launched another spacecraft that has rivaled Voyager 1. No other spacecraft has traveled as far; no other spacecraft is leaving the Solar System with as rapid a velocity; no current or even planned spacecraft is on track to ever overtake it. Voyager 1, the first spacecraft to exit the Solar System, is still the most distant, and looks to remain so for the foreseeable future. There’s a remarkable story behind this mission and how it achieved its record-breaking properties, and there’s an equally interesting story behind how we could someday catch or even surpass Voyager 1: if only we invested in doing so. This image shows Voyager 1 lifting off aboard the Titan III/Centaur rocket on September 5, 1977: joining its sister spacecraft, Voyager 2, which was launched 16 days prior. Voyager 1 was not the fastest spacecraft upon launch, but now on a trajectory out of the Solar System, has become the fastest-moving spacecraft away from the Sun: showcasing that initial speed is not everything when it comes to how far a craft can ultimately make it into the Universe. Credit : NASA Anytime you want to send anything to any place in space, you have two options for how to get it there once you launch it above Earth’s atmosphere. The first option is to use some sort of engine — something that provides thrust, like rocket fuel — to propel your spacecraft to the needed speed in the proper direction, i.e., with the right trajectory, to get there. The second option is to take advantage of the natural gravity of other objects that you’ll encounter, such as planets that orbit the Sun or moons that orbit planets, in order to provide an “assist” to your spacecraft. This gravity assist maneuver can, depending on how it’s leveraged, provide either an increase or a decrease in speed, and can also alter your trajectory significantly in the process. Of course, it’s possible to combine these two effects as well, in what’s known as either a powered flyby or the Oberth effect , to either gain or lose even more speed than using thrusters and gravity assists separately. When an object has a gravitational encounter with a planet within our Solar System, from the planet’s perspective, the object comes in and goes out in a speed-conserving interaction. However, since the planet is in motion relative to the Sun, its gravitational influence redirects the spacecraft in such a way that the planet’s motion, depending on whether it’s “with” or “against” the spacecraft’s relative motion, can either boost or de-boost the spacecraft relative to the Sun. This type of maneuver is known as a gravity assist. Credit : David Shortt, Rachelz9999/Wikimedia Commons In the case of Voyager 1, it was launched on September 5, 1977, with an initial speed of around 40 km/s: the equivalent of 89,500 miles-per-hour or 144,000 km/hr. Interestingly, that launch date and launch speed were both later and slower than its twin: Voyager 2. However, they were designed for different purposes. Voyager 2 was planned to fly by Jupiter and Saturn in a way that could potentially take it to Uranus and Neptune afterward (performing a “grand tour” of the Solar System), while Voyager 1 was designed to fly by Jupiter, Saturn, and then to get a choice between heading all the way out to Pluto or to fly close to Saturn’s giant moon Titan. Because of these differences, different initial speeds and trajectories were required for each of the Voyagers. Although Voyager 2 launched first and started out faster, it was passed by Voyager 1 on December 19th of 1977, as Voyager 1 headed on a more direct course toward Jupiter. On March 5, 1979, it arrived: Voyager 1 made a close approach of Jupiter , coming within 279,000 km of the edge of Jupiter’s atmosphere. It also flew by its moons Amalthea, Io (at a distance of just 20,570 km), Europa, and on March 6, by Ganymede and Callisto as well. Its views of Io, Ganymede, and Callisto, plus Jupiter, were the highest-resolution photos of those worlds ever taken. Its approach video to Jupiter remains one of the most iconic sequences in space history. This animation sequence shows Voyager 1’s approach of Jupiter in March of 1979. Its swirling winds, moving bands, and hurricane-like storm raging in its Great Red Spot were all revealed in detail that had never been seen before. During Voyager 1’s 1979 flyby encounter with Jupiter, a brief “point” of light was seen on Jupiter’s surface, representing the first observed bolide event in Jupiter’s atmosphere. Credit : NASA/JPL/Voyager 1 Another big surprise was the discovery of active volcanic activity on Io: now known to be the most volcanically active world in the Solar System. As Jupiter’s tidal forces continuously open cracks in Io’s crust and trigger massive volcanic eruptions, the entire world gets resurfaced on timescales of mere thousands of years, giving it the youngest surface in the entire Solar System. Io is the innermost of Jupiter’s four major Galilean moons, with the closest, tightest orbit around Jupiter of them all. Voyager 1 actually flew interior to Io’s orbit, passing just behind it mere hours after departing from its closest approach to Jupiter. However, there was another purpose to flying so close to Jupiter on the specific trajectory that was chosen: to boost Voyager 1’s speed and alter its trajectory to send it on to Saturn. When choosing how to direct the spacecraft, the decision was made to go after an extremely close approach to Saturn’s Titan, rather than to go on an extended mission to Pluto. The reason was scientifically motivated: because Titan was known to have an atmosphere, and a substantial one at that. Therefore, the thinking was, more science value could be extracted by flying by Titan than by eschewing that to go after Pluto. As a result of the close flyby to Jupiter, Voyager 1’s speed — which had dropped down to 13 km/s owing to the gravitational pull of the Sun as it sped away from it — shot back up to 23 km/s after receiving a near-maximal gravity assist. This animation shows the trajectory of Voyager 1, launched in 1977, as it received a gravity assist from Jupiter during its flyby and then another one from Saturn (and Titan) when it encountered that planet and its lunar system. Those two gravitational interactions boosted Voyager 1 to the highest escape speed of any human-made object ever, and after overtaking Pioneer 10 in 1998, it has remained our most distant spacecraft ever since. Credit : Phoenix7777/Wikimedia Commons A year and a half later, In November of 1980, Voyager 1 arrived at Saturn: double the distance from the Sun compared to Jupiter. Although its speed had slowed down to about 20 km/s owing to the continued, energy-draining climb out of the Sun’s gravitational potential well, it managed to pass incredibly close to Titan: passing within just 3915 km of its surface.
